name: Not Enough Water (Drought)
summary: Leaves droop or curl up during hot afternoons and leaf edges turn dry and brown because the soil is too dry.

immediateActions: Water deeply at the base of the plant early in the morning or late afternoon.
Cover the soil around stems with 5–8 cm of dry straw, coconut husk, or grass to hold moisture.
biologicalControl: Mix compost into the soil after harvest so it holds water longer next season.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Do NOT spray pest medicine or spread dry fertilizer while the plant is thirsty—it will burn the roots.
prevention: Use straw mulch and water deeply before soil starts cracking.

name: Too Much Water (Drowned Roots)
scientificName: Water Issue — Standing water suffocating roots
summary: Plant droops even though the soil is soggy or flooded; older bottom leaves turn dull yellow and roots rot.

immediateActions: Stop watering right away and dig small trenches to let standing rainwater drain out.
Loosen packed mud gently around the bed once the water goes down.
biologicalControl: Add dry compost once the soil drains so healthy roots can recover without rotting.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Do not pour extra sprays into wet soil until the field drains.
prevention: Plant vegetables, papaya, and pepper on raised beds (25–40 cm high) before rainy season.

name: Too Little Sunlight (Too Shady)
summary: Pale yellow-green leaves with tall, weak, thin stems and few flowers or fruits because trees or clouds block the sun.

immediateActions: Trim overhanging tree branches or thin out crowded plants so sunlight reaches the leaves.
Tie weak, tall stems gently to bamboo stakes so wind does not snap them.
biologicalControl: Hold back extra urea/nitrogen in shade, because it makes stems even softer and weaker.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: No spray needed—getting more sunlight brings back healthy dark-green leaves in 7–10 days.
prevention: Plant sun-loving crops (corn, tomato, chili, okra) in open sunny spots; keep shady areas for coffee, cacao, or pepper.

name: Too Much Fertilizer (Fertilizer Burn)
scientificName: Fertilizer Issue — Root & leaf salt burn
summary: Crisp brown burnt leaf tips and edges shortly after putting heavy urea/NPK or fresh animal manure near the stems.

immediateActions: Water the soil heavily with clean fresh water 2–3 times over 2 days to wash away excess fertilizer salts.
Brush away any fertilizer pellets sitting directly against the plant stem.
biologicalControl: Spread well-rotted compost or grass mulch once flushed to calm the soil.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Stop ALL fertilizer and leaf sprays for 2–3 weeks until new green leaves grow out.
prevention: Put fertilizer 8–10 cm away from stems, water right after applying, and age animal manure at least 2 months before use.

name: Weak Soil / Needs Plant Food
scientificName: Soil Food Issue — Low nitrogen or minerals
summary: Even yellowing across leaves without bugs or mold: older bottom leaves turn yellow (needs nitrogen) or have burnt edges (needs potassium).

immediateActions: Feed a balanced NPK fertilizer or rich compost + wood ash around the roots and water it in well.
Check whether bottom older leaves or top new leaves are yellowing to pick the right plant food.
biologicalControl: Mix compost, vermicast, or cover crops like mungbean into beds between harvests to rebuild tired soil.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: If leaves stay yellow between green veins, a light morning zinc/magnesium leaf feed helps recovery.
prevention: Feed small split doses through the season and add agricultural lime if soil is too sour/acidic.

name: Sunburn / Extreme Heat
summary: Dry white or papery tan sunken patches on the sunny side of tomatoes, chilies, papayas, or top leaves during very hot weather.

immediateActions: Put temporary shade net (30–40% shade) or palm fronds over nursery beds and tender fruit crops during heatwaves.
Avoid trimming too many top leaves that protect growing fruits from the afternoon sun.
biologicalControl: Keep straw mulch thick and soil moist so plants can cool themselves naturally.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Do NOT spray oil or sulfur sprays when afternoon heat goes above 34°C—they worsen sunburn.
prevention: Leave enough upper leaves to shade fruits and water early in the morning.

name: Weedkiller Spray Drift Damage
scientificName: Spray Issue — Weedkiller blew from nearby
summary: Curled, twisted narrow new leaves or sudden white-yellow bleached spots after weedkiller was sprayed nearby—without insects.

immediateActions: If weedkiller drifted within the last 1–2 hours, wash the leaves gently with clean water right away.
Water the roots lightly and let new healthy side-shoots grow out before trimming dead tips.
biologicalControl: Wait until fresh normal leaves emerge before cutting off twisted tips.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Wash sprayer tanks 3 times with soap and clean water after weedkiller—keep a separate sprayer just for crops.
prevention: Spray weeds only on calm mornings with no wind, keeping the nozzle low near the ground.

name: Salty or Sour Soil Problem
scientificName: Soil Issue — Coastal salt or acid buildup
summary: White-burnt leaf tips and stunted patches near salty coastal water, or rusty-orange older rice leaves on sour acid soil.

immediateActions: For salty fields: flush beds with fresh rainwater/canal water and repair bunds to block brackish tide water.
For rusty rice in sour soil: drain the paddy for 3–5 days to let air reach the roots.
biologicalControl: Spread agricultural lime or rice-husk ash/biochar with potassium fertilizer to balance sour soil.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Avoid ammonium sulfate fertilizer on sour soils; use urea paired with potassium.
prevention: Choose salt-tolerant local varieties if farming near river deltas or coastal areas.

name: Wind or Storm Damage
scientificName: Weather Issue — Torn or bent by wind
summary: Straight torn strips on banana or corn leaves, snapped stems, or leaning plants right after strong wind—without worms or bug droppings.

immediateActions: Prop up bent stalks gently with stakes and cut cleanly across broken branches so rot does not enter.
Drain standing storm rainwater out of beds right away.
biologicalControl: For valuable fruit trees (durian, mango, cacao), clean broken bark and cover big cuts after storms.
recommendations.chemicalGuidance: Do not spray worm medicine for wind-torn leaves—check for real worms or droppings first.
prevention: Plant bamboo or fast-growing windbreak trees along the windy side of banana and orchard plots.
